analysis.one_liner: Lets voters and the Justice Department sue to keep insurrection participants off ballots.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2022 with a single cosponsor, the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Attorney General or individual voters sue in federal court to have anyone who took part in or aided the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack declared disqualified from federal or state office under the 14th Amendment, and to keep that person's name off the ballot. It declares the January 6 attack an insurrection and defines "participant" broadly, covering people who were unlawfully inside the Capitol, funded or directed the breach, incited others to enter, or had authority to stop the attack and failed to act. A state election official who placed a disqualified candidate on a ballot could be fined or imprisoned up to a year. The bill never advanced past a House Judiciary subcommittee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain a real enforcement tool for a constitutional rule — the 14th Amendment's bar on insurrectionists holding office — that otherwise depends on scattered, case-by-case lawsuits. The Attorney General gains explicit statutory authority to investigate and sue, and candidates running against disqualified rivals would benefit from their removal from the ballot.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting insurrection participants off ballots

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal court path — a three-judge panel on an expedited schedule, with appeal directly to the Supreme Court — for the Attorney General or an eligible voter to have a candidate declared disqualified under the 14th Amendment and kept off federal and state ballots.

Declares the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack an insurrection and defines "participant" to include people unlawfully inside the Capitol, those who funded, directed, or incited the breach, and officials who had authority to halt the attack but knowingly failed or refused to do so.
Sets a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, a lower bar than the 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard in criminal cases, making disqualification easier to prove than a crime.
Makes it a federal crime, punishable by a fine or up to one year in prison, for a state's chief election official to place a judicially disqualified candidate on a ballot.

analysis.who_pays: Candidates found to be insurrection participants would lose ballot access and eligibility for federal and state office. The Justice Department would bear the cost of investigations and litigation, taxpayers would fund the expedited three-judge court proceedings, and state election officials would face fines and possible prison terms if they listed a disqualified name.
analysis.who_pays_short: Disqualified candidates, state election officials, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill declares one specific event — the January 6 attack — to be an insurrection by statute and would disqualify people without requiring any individual criminal conviction, raising due-process concerns about courts labeling people insurrectionists through a civil case on a lowered standard of proof.

Its definition of "participant" is sweeping: someone merely present in the Capitol without authorization who "should have known" their actions would disrupt Congress could face lifetime disqualification from office, forcing judges to decide contested questions of knowledge and intent in fast-tracked proceedings.

Because it names only the January 6 attack and its participants, critics would view it as aimed at one party's politicians rather than a neutral insurrection statute, inviting claims of political weaponization of ballot access.
Keeping candidates off the ballot removes choices from the voters who might want to support them — a real cost to voter choice, even if grounded in a constitutional disqualification provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given voters and the Justice Department a genuine enforcement mechanism for a constitutional rule that today depends on ad hoc litigation, and its criminal penalty for election officials adds teeth. But its design is blunt: a retroactive, event-specific definition of "participant" that reaches people never convicted of a crime, applied under a low civil standard of proof and aimed at keeping names off ballots. A more careful version would have tied disqualification to individual adjudicated findings of insurrection. The core goal — enforcing the 14th Amendment against officials who tried to subvert an election — is sound; the drafting invited years of constitutional fights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Constitution subcommittee, and never got a markup or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz introduced the bill on May 27, 2022, with Rep. Jamie Raskin as its only cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On November 1, 2022, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded after that.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired in committee without any floor action in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Politicians and candidates who took part in or aided the January 6, 2021 attack are better off: no federal statutory mechanism now exists to disqualify them under the 14th Amendment, and their ballot eligibility is unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Politicians tied to January 6 kept eligibility

for.name: Debbie Wasserman Schultz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a civil action for 14th Amendment disqualification of insurrection participants.

for.name: Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee, was sent to the Constitution subcommittee on November 1, 2022, and he never scheduled a markup or committee vote; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so no partisan split on the merits was ever measured.

industries.industry: Politicians and candidates who participated in or aided the January 6 attack
industries.note: The bill would have allowed courts to bar them from federal and state ballots under the 14th Amendment's insurrection clause; because it died, they retain full eligibility and the only checks on them remain criminal prosecution or ad hoc lawsuits.

Had it passed, a state's chief election official who placed a disqualified candidate on a ballot would have committed a federal crime carrying a fine or up to a year in prison — new personal legal exposure, though in service of enforcing a public rule.
